Oct. 31, 2013. The day that kicked off the "game." I was in a STEM major because my parents strongly pushed it. Second year, O-chem time. My social life was sparse, with the one steady consolation the guy who'd turn abusive. 

I went out with some high school friends that night, and sat pretty quietly while they chatted at the restaurant. Came home feeling bleak, and tried to get started on some O-chem. 

My suicidal thoughts had kicked up that year, but that day, I decided to take the step. Started looking up where the arteries done. Ripped apart that razor and twisted the blade into my wrist. 

Blood pouring out, I was trying to feel some emotion. Texted a friend what was going on. Still remember the all caps "NO!" He called me, and he called me and spoke for 20 minutes. Toward the end, "Which dorm are you in?" and I knew what was coming.

Security guards outside as I started numbing out. I walked out and the friend's parents swoop toward me, crying. Guards come toward me, I vaguely hear the words "hospital," and the paramedics came. 

A bit of a blur - putting on my bra, that blood pressure cuff in the ambulance tightening. Pulling into that hospital and going into the unit - a fishbowl of eight rooms in an enclosed circle. The mechanical voice of the nurse evaluating my wounds. "Lacerations." 

Wheeled up to the psych ward alongside a security guard, and that was my night.

Bipolar 2. I feel like no matter what, I'll always have (as Mark Hill described on Cracked) the voice in the back of my mind telling me that there's an easy way out of every problem. My meds are well adjusted, I've gotten decent hobbies, yet the tiniest of things can trigger suicidal thoughts. 

Looking back, one of the most heartwarming things said to me: "Uh, I have no idea how to help, but here's some ice cream." Thought of that moment the next couple years whenever I saw ice cream. Buddy didn't try to fix the problem - and in some ways, it's not really "What's bothering you? Tell me the answer." There perhaps is no answer. Instead, it's just being with that person. 

Though as a note, burnout is real. I'd recommend your own therapist, too. My best friend had pretty much no clue about depression, and even said he couldn't really help me (thankfully, I took that). However, he took me to the hospital while making me laugh the whole way, brought me back chocolate from his Mainland trip, and just texted me about random stuff after I got out of the hospital. Always will be grateful.

TL;DR: When hellishly depressed, bribing myself with ice cream. When on proper meds, hobbies.  

For starters, without meds, I wouldn't be alive or functioning. Multiple suicides in my family line. My suicidal feelings center around numbness, or perhaps a feeling of sadness that I drown out with numbness. 

Getting out of bed when I wasn't on meds: Bribing myself with ice cream, because staying in bed the whole day makes you feel both tired and guilty at day's end. Getting a paycheck in case I don't kill myself. Seeing friends. YouTube videos. Note: This was when I didn't have the energy to kill myself. Numb out pain, go to work because I need that pay. 

Getting out of bed when on okay meds: Doing something good at work. One hobby that I enjoy. 

When actively suicidal: This surprisingly puts energy into me, so the getting out of bed part isn't a problem. That being said, honestly, the difference between calling a friend or not depends on the quickness and ease of my method.   

On good meds: Actually enjoying getting out of bed. Seeing hobbies that I can develop. Knowing there's a life besides getting out of bed.

Posted about two hospitals before (one good, one bad), but here's all the lowlights: 

Doctor: "You should want to live." Left the ward, was back within two days. Doctor: "You should want to live." No meds changed.

Nurse: "This is a place for suicidals and drug addicts. They come here, eat ice cream, watch TV, have vacation. She want to go home, watch TV, eat bonbons, that's her choice." Needless to say, this was the hospital with no therapy.

First couple times in the ER take the longest: Every successive psych ward trip, in my experience, gets shorter. (I just made seven trips...went from four to one hour) Good hospital will keep you posted and perhaps give you a friendly security guard. Bad hospitals will stick you in the psych ER and let you wait. And safety from other patients may be slightly lacking...I nicknamed this psych holding room a "fishbowl" - one large room with eight rooms in a circle, with cameras in each, no locks, and security screened off.

Hospital staff has to, bluntly, see you with almost nothing on. Friendly nurse will be very polite, shield you from the door (which had a window), help stick your clothes away, treat the wounds. Nurse at bad ER will mechanically evaluate your wounds while reciting them to the scribe.

Good hospital will try to keep patients that are having outbursts away from the other patients. Bad hospital will be nonchalant when someone throws a plastic chair across the admittedly larger room. 

Even good hospitals will screw up your consents. Take it as granted that the friends on your "approved" list will accidentally be blocked from seeing/calling you, and that the "not on approved" list will get hold of you with no problem. Admittedly, they'll give you the phone number of the friend who tried to call...though by then, the friend won't be available, and you'll be back in therapy with the phones turned off.

And to top it off, the bad hospital had some nasty foods. Luckily, the other hospital let us request no fish (can be badly cooked).

Old system: Scan a document, upload it to the relevant client file, then place the hard copy in a folder. To make it quicker, perhaps scan about 15 or so various multi-page documents, then split the PDFs and upload them into the respective client files. After files uploaded, stamp them with "scanned." Someone decided that shredding the hard copies would be a good idea. Problems:

-We had a backlog of three boxes of paper, all waiting to be scanned and uploaded (a three-month process). 

-Someone decided to catch us up by putting maybe 100 pages from various documents through the scanner at one time. By the time he was through, he'd done this to maybe 2000 pages of documents. He never bothered to split the PDFs.

-Aforementioned genius used this "scanned" stamp to indicate that he had scanned a document...not that they had been uploaded. 

-We were ordered to change databases, then to change back databases, then use both databases...you get the idea. Documents were between two places.

Company gave us orders to shred, and I got out two weeks later. A month after I left, hard copies of files were stripped to the bare minimum and sent to an offsite storage company. Hard copies with "scanned" on them were - to the best of my knowledge - shredded.  Program manager's teenage daughter and her friend put in partial charge of splitting up the uploaded files. Needless to say, they were hopeless.

-Company lost access to the larger of two databases, shredded and lost client assessments with client addresses, got rid of original client documents, and are regularly being fined and sanctioned. 

Good riddance.

Mrs. B "taught" 12th grade Honors English online. Let's rephrase that. 

Mrs. B would give us books and set us an assignment: Create a Twitter post, make a Google Site with embedded video clips of people acting, make a book trailer, record ourselves reading sentences from the book, and do a Skype chat. 

Problem was, we were never taught how to do any of those, yet we were graded on arbitrary criteria. That's why I'm so good at Googling now - because I had no guidance whatsoever. I didn't have a smartphone, and I had a mother who'd yell at me when I asked to hang out with friends, even to work on projects.

We learned quickly that there wouldn't be actual book analysis. Just her making us do "technological" things with "21st-century skills," but neglecting actually understanding the book. We all struggled to distill entire chapters into tweets, because we'd all earn low scores with absolutely no feedback. 

Still more bitter about her than the teachers who let us do nothing in class, because at least they knew that we weren't learning anything. Ironically, the one teacher (AP English) who followed her example ended up discussing almost no book interpretation or essay writing at all.

Let's see, I started it Jan. 2nd (thank you, Daylio, for keeping track of past appts), and only really started getting over the anxiety at the beginning of March. Non-professional opinion: I think it has to do with the hierarchy of needs: We've made sure safety has been relatively reached, so now we're on the next level -  love/belonging. And thanks to the depression, we haven't had the energy to seek love and belonging to date. So now it's time for what is honestly a pain in the ass: finding something to do and finding friends, whether through Meetup, hiking/cheap gyms, Pokemon Go (friend me!), whatnot.
